editorial.headline: Shariah Bullion Banking: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Shariah-compliant banking for taking precious-metal deposits and lending the metal is nationally open to foreign investment, yet PMA registration at a Bali address is blocked.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register this activity at a Bali address today. Nationally, it is classified as open to foreign investment, with a maximum foreign ownership ceiling of 100%. But Bali’s position is different: the activity is closed to PMA registration under the province-wide moratorium.

The activity is shariah-compliant bullion banking. Its core work is to accept deposits of precious metals—such as gold or silver—held as bars or currency, and to extend loans in those precious metals under shariah principles. The point is not simply the metal itself, but a banking activity built around receiving it on deposit and lending it onward within that stated framework.

The registration is available across every listed business scale: micro, small, medium and large. That breadth matters nationally because the foreign-investment position is not presented as a partial opening at only one of those scales. A business structured around this defined bullion-banking activity can therefore find a nationally open PMA route, including full foreign ownership within the stated national ceiling.

Bali changes the practical answer. At the large-business scale, this activity is recorded as low risk. Bali’s permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium blocks all low- and medium-low-risk activities from PMA registration at a Bali address. The restriction is not a reduced local ownership allowance or a Bali-specific percentage cap: it is a bar on PMA registration for this activity in Bali. The governing basis cited is a governor’s letter issued in May 2026. For founders, the distinction is decisive: national openness remains real, but it does not create a PMA registration path in Bali while this moratorium applies.
